name: Kaonde / Kikaonde
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wright, J.L. 2007. An Outline of Kikaonde Grammar. (Series editor Mubanga E. Kashoki.) Lusaka: Bookworld Publishers and UNZA Press. ISBN 978-9982-24-04-99.
catalog_locator: Ch. I Phonology, section 'Stress', printed p. 9 (p. 10 of an a copy whose provenance we do not cite; scanned image, no text)
catalog_quote: Stress. In every Kaonde word at least one syllable is spoken with slightly more force than the others, though this is not so marked as in English. This syllable is said to be stressed. Sometimes a word may also have a secondary stress on another syllable. It is probably true that in the majority of words this stress falls on the next to last syllable, but there are so many exceptions to this that it cannot be stated as a rule. Stress can come on any syllable including the last in contrast with English. Kaonde stress is independent of tone. A stressed syllable may be high or low and a high syllable may be stressed or unstressed. Some random examples follow in which the stressed syllable is underlined and the high tones marked: muuntu 'person', kijiilo 'feast', kilújo 'right hand', kalómbwana 'little boy', mujilo 'fire', pémbela 'wait', lánguluka 'think', mulanguluko 'through', lukétekelo…

tone_statements.citation: Kashoki, Mubanga E. and Michael Mann. 1978. A general sketch of the Bantu languages of Zambia. In: Sirarpi Ohannessian and Mubanga E. Kashoki (eds.), Language in Zambia, 47-100. London: International African Institute. [whole-book scanned PDF open at UNZA DSpace,http://dspace.unza.zm/handle/123456789/939]
tone_statements.quote: In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed … stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish vvords from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of ali Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone. … tone refers to a (voice) pitch (a kind of musical note) on the individual syilable. There are only tvvo contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low, vvhich serve to distinguish … between words which are otherwise identical in ali other respects.
tone_statements.summary: Survey statement for all Zambian languages incl. Kaonde: every syllable carries tone, only two contrastive tones, high and low; stress even and never distinctive; highs lower toward sentence end.

tone_statements.citation: Wright, J. L. and N. Kamukwamba. 1958. Kaonde note book: with an elementary grammar of the language. [London]: Longmans, Green (published in association with the Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland Publications Bureau). 60 pp.
tone_statements.quote: 正書沼ではアクセント表記をしないことになっているが,ここでは,高く発音きされる母音の上に/を付して低い母音と区別する。また高い母音のあとの母音もしくは子音前鼻音に高い場合と低い場合があると解釈されるので子音前鼻音も`の有無で区刃する。 … また,語末の高い音箔は下降調で発音されることが多いが, `高」と`下限」の区初があるとしうる根拠も見っつかっていないので, `であらわす。 … カオンデ語の動詞は,他の多くのパントッ諸語同様,アクセントの面で②つの型に分けられ,その差異は不定形にちいてもあらわれる。
tone_statements.translation: The orthography does not mark accent, but here an acute is placed over a vowel pronounced high to distinguish it from a low vowel. Further, since the vowel or pre-consonantal nasal that follows a high vowel is interpreted as being either high or low, the pre-consonantal nasal too is distinguished by presence or absence of the acute. ... Also, a word-final high syllable is often pronounced with a falling pitch, but as no grounds have been found for positing a distinction between 'high' and 'falling', it is written with the acute. ... Kaonde verbs, as in many other Bantu languages, divide into two types with respect to accent, and the difference shows up in the infinitive as well.
tone_statements.locator: p.150, はじめに (transcription conventions), and p.152, §1-1 不定形
tone_statements.summary: Each vowel and moraic nasal is high or low; a word-final high is often realised falling but no high/falling contrast is found; verb stems fall into two lexical tone types (peaked vs flat).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim on printed p. 9 of the Wright 2007 scan we hold; citation and ISBN match the imprint page. (2) Deciding source: a 55-page missionary grammar sketch (1977, reissued 2007 under Kashoki's editorship) with an impressionistic stress paragraph ('probably true that in the majority of words..'). Against Glottolog's 35-item bibliography, CrossRef, archive.org, HAL/theses.fr and the UNZA repository, nothing fuller exists: no reference grammar, no phonology monograph, no JIPA illustration, no instrumental study; so Wright is the best available and is. (3) Why 'thin' rather than 'adequate': every other description read treats Kaonde as tone + length with no word stress - Kashoki 1978 (held, Language in Zambia pp. 70-71: syllables 'more or less evenly stressed', penult force possibly an artefact of lengthening, stress never distinctive
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: quotation verified in source. Re-opened (p.10 = printed pp.8-9 of). Printed p.9, heading 'Stress', reads verbatim as the record's quote from 'In every Kaonde word at least one syllable is spoken with slightly more force..' through '..Some random examples follow in which the stressed syllable is underlined and the high tones marked: muuntu 'person', kijiilo 'feast', kilújo..'; the record's ellipsis only truncates the example list (continues 'lukétekelo 'trust' some say luketekeelo, jiké 'egg', bútemwe 'love', 'goodness', mulokazhi 'daughter-in-la

sources.citation: Mambwe, Kelvin. 2012 [2008]. Some linguistic variations of Kaonde: a dialectological study. MA dissertation, University of Zambia (HELD image-only PDF; sec. 3.4 scanned now, one page at a time, 300 dpi).
sources.quote: 'Kaonde language has two suprasegmental features, these are, tone and length.' Two level tones H/L (contour only on long syllables), lexical tone and length minimal pairs (maana/maana; malwa/maalwa). No mention of stress anywhere in the phonology chapter.
